title: How To Drastically Improve Your Class
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin shares what he calls a secret known only to a small percentage of teachers despite its simplicity: whenever students fail to meet expectations, stop them immediately, reteach the expectation, and begin again. He explains that the strategy only works when applied consistently every single time, since inconsistent use confuses students and signals that the teacher doesn't mean what they say. Committing fully to the approach, he argues, forces the teacher to become far more effective at initial instruction while training students to become tenacious, active listeners, holding both parties accountable. He acknowledges the approach can be slow going at first, especially mid-year, requiring teachers to repeat instruction they might otherwise assume students already understood, but promises that persistence eventually produces a class that translates instructions into action almost automatically, freeing up significant time.
points: A simple, consistently applied secret—stop, reteach, begin again whenever expectations aren't met—can dramatically improve a class.
The strategy only works if applied every single time; inconsistent use confuses students and undermines the teacher's credibility.
Commitment to the approach forces teachers to become more effective at initial instruction, not just more strict with consequences.
Adopting the strategy mid-year can be slow initially, since students accustomed to half-listening require extensive repetition at first.
Sustained use eventually produces students who translate instructions into action with minimal repetition, freeing significant classroom time.
quotes: If ever your students aren’t giving you what you want . . . Stop them in their tracks. Reteach your expectations. Begin again.
Trotting it out every once in a while—or even more often than not—is not only confusing to students, but it sends the message that you don’t really mean what you say.
The strategy works because it forces you, as a natural consequence, to become extraordinarily effective with your initial instruction.
Your students may be so used to half listening, or not listening at all, that you'll have to repeat nearly everything you do.
Your students will realize that when you give an instruction, when you teach and model what you want in explicit detail, or just make a simple request, you really do mean for them to follow it.
It starts with an all-or-nothing commitment to mean what you say, to make your actions congruent with your words.
